newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: WTO chief to visit China to push entry talks.
newsitem.headline: WTO chief to visit China to push entry talks.

text.p: World Trade Organisation (WTO) director-general Renato Ruggiero said on Thursday he was planning to visit China in mid-April to try to help speed up Beijing's long-stalled admission to the 130-member body.

His trip, details of which have yet to be finalised, will come soon after a fresh round of talks starting in Geneva next week between senior Chinese negotiators and officials of key WTO powers, including the European Union and the United States.
"My aim is to make a personal contribution to promoting the negotiations," Ruggiero told reporters.
He sees the earliest possible entry of China, Russia, Ukraine and Taiwan as one of the trade body's key priorities.

Trade sources said Ruggiero was expected to tour not only areas of China which have flourished under economic liberalisation but also less-advanced regions that Beijing uses to try to justify its claim to get WTO entry as a developing country.
If this were granted, it would allow Beijing more time to adjust its trade practices to the WTO's internationally-agreed rules for open world trade.
Ruggiero says it is vital to bring in China and Russia -- which is not seeking developing country status -- to give the increasingly influential organisation truly global cover.

But he has insisted that Beijing must satisfy other countries that it has adjusted its long state-controlled economic system enough -- or will do so within a short time-frame -- to ensure it conforms with the rules.
Last week, new U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright discussed the WTO entry issue with China's President Jiang Zemin, Prime Minister Li Peng and Foreign Minister Qian Qichen.

Although she gave no indication of their response, Deputy U.S. Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang told a Congressional group in Washington on Wednesday that he doubted an entry agreement for China would evolve in the near term.

Negotiations in Geneva, which began a decade ago but were suspended in the early 1990s following China's suppression of a democracy movement, had still not gone very far, Lang said, according to a text issued by the U.S. mission in Geneva.
"China maintains many trade barriers that must be eliminated, and we need to ensure the necessary changes are made before accession occurs.
"The pace of China's accession negotiations depends very much on Beijing's wilingness to improve the offers now on the table," Lang told a House of Representatives trade sub-committee.

In January, the office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR), equivalent to a foreign trade ministry, issued a list of barriers to trade in goods and services which it said still faced foreign companies dealing with China.

Although last month Beijing was reported to have pledged in talks with U.S. officials it would take further steps to open up its domestic market, trade diplomats in Geneva said there had been little sign of fresh movement so far.

They said the first indication of any possible shift could come on March 6 when the WTO working party on China's accession, which last met in October last year, discusses the latest offers from Beijing.

Long Yongtu, Beijing's main negotiator and an assistant minister of foreign trade, will address the session. He is also expected to have bilateral discussions with U.S., EU and Japanese trade diplomats.
